abstract: The generation of reward incentive value and maintenance of motivational drive are distinct processes in reward-related behavior. However, how neural circuits differentially process these components remains poorly understood. Although intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) paradigms have been utilized to identify reward-related circuits, ICSS measures may conflate reinitiated actions attributed to learned incentive value with ongoing motivated behavior sustained by concurrent stimulation. Here, we reveal a dissociation between these processes by optogenetically stimulating fibers in the stria terminalis bundle projecting to the medial nucleus accumbens (STBmNAc) and those in the medial forebrain bundle originating from the lateral NAc (MFBlNAc). We found that STBmNAc stimulation facilitated the reinitiation of ICSS actions, whereas MFBlNAc stimulation sustained ongoing ICSS behavior. Moreover, shortening the stimulation duration in STBmNAc mice increased the likelihood of subsequent re-engagement of stimulation-seeking. Additionally, STBmNAc stimulation, but not MFBlNAc stimulation, could substitute for primary rewards and support the acquisition of sensory cue-dependent operant behavior. Together, our findings suggest that STBmNAc activation promotes reward-anticipatory behavior by conferring reward incentive value, whereas MFBlNAc activation sustains ongoing behavior by maintaining motivational drive. Thus, reward-related behavior may not be governed by a unitary motivational system but may involve anatomically and functionally distinct neural components.
